extracted.intended_audience: USPTO practitioners, counsel and parties in USPTO disciplinary appeals and enforcement proceedings (OED/OHA attorneys and regulated practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing motions, stays, reconsideration, sanctions, and ethical-rule violations in USPTO disciplinary proceedings and appeals to the USPTO Director. Applies to filing, timing, conferral, burdens of proof, and sanctioning analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission required to file briefs or motions in hearing appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: No briefs or motions are permitted in hearing appeals without permission of the USPTO Director. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.55(m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must seek leave before filing briefs or motions in appeals to the USPTO Director; filing without leave can be rejected as unauthorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion confer requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(o))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every motion must include a statement that the moving party or attorney for the moving party has conferred with the opposing party or attorney for the opposing party in a good faith effort to resolve the issues raised by the motion and whether the motion is opposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions lacking the required conferral statement or representation that counsel were notified may be denied on procedural grounds; the Order repeatedly denies motions for failure to comply with § 11.55(o).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion response and reply time limits (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(o))
rubrics_metrics.description: [W]ithin 21 days of the date of service of the motion, an opposing party shall serve and file a response to the motion, and the moving party may file a reply within 14 days after service of the opposing party's responsive memorandum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses filed after 21 days can be treated as untimely; moving parties' replies must be within 14 days of the response. Timeliness is a standalone basis for granting or denying motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration filing deadline and stay effect (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a final decision of the USPTO Director, either party may make a single request for reconsideration or modification of the decision by the USPTO Director if filed within 20 days from the date of entry of the decision. Such a request shall have the effect of staying the effective date of the order of discipline in the final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A timely § 11.56(c) request stays the effective date of discipline; only one such request is permitted and must be filed within 20 days to obtain the statutorily described stay effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for reconsideration under § 11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: No request for reconsideration or modification shall be granted unless the request is based on newly discovered evidence or error of law or fact, and the requestor must demonstrate that any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered any earlier by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconsideration is a narrow remedy reserved for new evidence or errors of law/fact. Requests that merely rehash prior arguments, raise points that could have been presented earlier, or express disagreement with the decision are inappropriate. The Order cites the federal Rules 59(e)/60 principles and cases (e.g., Hutchinson, Boryan) as persuasive analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for reconsideration (analogy to FRCP 59/60)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of review used by federal courts for motions to alter or amend a judgment under Rules 59(e) and 60 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure are most similar to requests for reconsideration filed pursuant to § 11.56(c). These standards are narrow and limited to new evidence or correction of errors of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency practice looks to FRCP authority: courts construe such motions narrowly; newly discovered evidence must not have been available prior to the decision; mere disagreement is insufficient (cases: Hutchinson v. Staton; Boryan v. United States; Above the Belt, Durkin, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional-circumstances requirement for stays (37 C.F.R. § 11.57(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as provided for in § 11.56(c), an order for discipline in a final decision will not be stayed except on proof of exceptional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 11.57(c) requires proof of exceptional circumstances to justify a stay; ordinary pending litigation or investigations do not ordinarily satisfy this standard. The USPTO has interpreted § 11.3(a) (extraordinary situations) as implying only extreme events (e.g., 'flood or fire') qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-situation/waiver (37 C.F.R. § 11.3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: [I]n an extraordinary situation, when justice requires, any requirement of the regulations of this Part which is not a requirement of statute may be suspended or waived by the USPTO Director or the designee of the USPTO Director, sua sponte, or on petition by any party ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's prior orders equate 'extraordinary' with catastrophic events; routine lawsuits or investigations are insufficient absent strong proof. The Order cites In re Schindler as requiring something like 'flood or fire.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence, and the respondent bears the burden of proving any affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate evidentiary standard; the tribunal applies this standard to evaluate allegations of misconduct and respondent defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions determination factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sanctions, USPTO regulations require the Tribunal to consider: (1) whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal commonly consults the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance on severity, length of sanction, and identification of aggravating/mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors for sanctions (illustrative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of aggravating factors include: a prior disciplinary offense; a pattern of misconduct; multiple violations; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary process; refusal to acknowledge the wrongful nature of the misconduct; and substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of these factors supports more severe sanctions (e.g., exclusion). The Order applies these factors (including a 1999 suspension) to justify exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA Standards § 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential mitigating factors are those enumerated in the ABA Standards § 9.32 (e.g., absence of prior disciplinary record, personal or emotional problems, full and free disclosure, restitution, remorse, timely good-faith effort to make restitution, cooperation with disciplinary proceedings, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigating factors, if established, can reduce the severity of sanctions; absence of mitigating factors weighs toward harsher discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against using reconsideration to relitigate or rehash prior arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration is not a vehicle to state a party's disagreement with a final judgment or to relitigate matters or introduce evidence that could have been previously presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities emphasize that mere disagreement (Hutchinson) or rehashing arguments is insufficient; motions must show new evidence or clear error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and example of 'prejudicial to the administration of justice' (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct is prejudicial to the administration of justice when it negatively impacts the public's perception of the courts or legal profession or undermines public confidence in the legal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forgery or filing documents with forged signatures or materially false submissions to USPTO can meet this standard (Order cites forgery of applicant signatures as an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of dishonesty, deceit, and falsification (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must be honest; conduct involving dishonesty, deceit, or misrepresentation violates § 11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include fabricating documents or evidence (fake 'Acknowledgement Receipt'), creating false client correspondence or unsent emails, or altering filings to mislead clients or the tribunal; such conduct supports findings of intentional misconduct and severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner duties to clients under USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner duties include competent and diligent representation (§§ 11.101, 11.103), abiding by client decisions (§ 11.102), keeping clients reasonably informed and explaining matters (§ 11.104(a)(3), (b)), communicating fees (§ 11.105(b)), holding client funds in trust and keeping them separate (§ 11.115(a),(c)), and protecting clients' interests on termination (§ 11.116(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of these duties (e.g., failing to file required patent applications, commingling client funds, failing to forward office actions) support disciplinary charges and inform sanction severity under § 11.54(b)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failing procedural prerequisites for motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to seek leave to file motions in appeals, or failure to comply with procedural requirements (e.g., conferral statement) are valid bases for denying motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order denied multiple motions on procedural grounds where no leave was sought and the § 11.55(o) conferral statement was omitted; previous warnings about compliance can weigh against movant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for motions to disqualify or strike (need authority and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions seeking disqualification or striking of opposing counsel must be supported by binding authority and evidence of the alleged conflict or misconduct; unsupported assertions or a jumble of allegations are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order denied a motion to disqualify where the movant provided no proof or controlling authority and only advanced unsupported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate brief deadlines and effect of failure to file (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(d) implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate briefs have prescribed filing deadlines (e.g., brief due date referenced), and failure to file timely may result in dismissal of the appeal if movant cannot show good cause or other statutory basis to extend or stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof that the record was served, reasonable access attempts, and compliance with motion rules are relevant to requests for extension; unexplained or unsupported failure to file is grounds for dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing and service requirements for reconsideration and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for reconsideration under § 11.56(c) must be filed within 20 days and served on specified USPTO offices/attorneys (General Counsel, and counsel for OED Director as provided). Judicial review is available under 35 U.S.C. § 32 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia within 30 days after the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the required service addresses and methods (mail or hand-delivery instructions provided). Failure to serve properly may affect timeliness or jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of federal court precedents and FRCP as persuasive guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure are not directly applicable in administrative proceedings, courts and USPTO have looked to Rules 59(e) and 60 and federal case law for guidance on standards (e.g., reconsideration standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order cites multiple federal cases and prior USPTO precedents to interpret § 11.56(c) and related standards; practitioners should cite analogous federal authority when appropriate but must meet the administrative regulation text.
